strengths: Novel and clearly motivated framing: generalizing the probabilistic adversarial attack framework of Zhang et al. [49] from a single image to a concept (a set of images or a generative model) is a natural, well-articulated extension, and the paper convincingly positions it relative to prior unrestricted attacks (ACA, DiffAttack, Song et al. [38]).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation for this line of work: white-box targeted attack, transferability across 8 classifiers including adversarially trained defenses, six no-reference image quality metrics, CLIP similarity, a user study with published annotator instructions, ablations on |C_ori| and M, and additional surrogate models (MobileNetV2, ViT-Base) in the appendix.

The results consistently support the central claim: concept-based attacks substantially improve white-box targeted success (97.82% vs 59.23% for ProbAttack) and aggressive-strategy transferability, while achieving the best user-study similarity and image-quality scores.

Honest treatment of limitations (per-concept fine-tuning cost, concept-constraint trade-off), broader impact discussion, dataset licensing, compute details, and a code repository, which supports reproducibility.
Useful methodological details: common random numbers and likelihood correction for variance reduction in Monte Carlo KL estimation are practical contributions on their own.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is thin. Theorem 1 is a straightforward calculus fact about KL to a Gaussian, and Theorem 2 is essentially an algebraic rearrangement of the KL definition. The Gaussian assumption on distance distributions in image space is strong and unjustified; the theory provides limited genuine insight beyond intuition already present in [49].

The empirical KL analysis (Section 5.3, Table 3) relies on diffusion-model likelihoods estimated via ELBO, which are known to be unreliable for comparing models, and the 'likelihood correction' of Appendix B rests on an unverified symmetry assumption; the very large variance of Δ estimates for some concepts (e.g., bear_plushie, shiny_sneaker, poop_emoji) weakens the claimed confirmation.

The experimental scale is small: only 26 concepts from DreamBoothPlus and 30 randomly selected target classes (780 adversarial examples). Findings on concept-heavy, object-centric categories may not generalize to natural image distributions.

White-box results are boosted by best-of-M selection with rejection sampling (M=10), which the strongest baselines (ACA, DiffAttack, NCF) do not use; a best-of-M comparison for these baselines would make the white-box numbers more convincing.

The practical threat model is questionable: the attack requires a curated concept dataset and ~8 hours of per-concept diffusion fine-tuning on an H100, so its applicability in realistic black-box/adaptive scenarios is unclear. The heavy compute cost is acknowledged but not analyzed.

The conservative strategy, which best preserves the concept, offers transferability only roughly comparable to DiffAttack; most of the transferability gains come from the aggressive strategy, whose concept fidelity is lower (CLIP score 0.8043 vs ProbAttack's 0.8581), creating a tension between the two headline claims.

CLIP similarity results are inconsistent across tables (e.g., OURS (CONS) scores below ProbAttack in Table 2 while the user study is claimed to show the opposite), and no statistical significance testing is reported for the user study with only five annotators.

strengths: The concept-level attack framing is a genuinely interesting extension of unrestricted adversarial attacks: rather than perturbing one image, the paper defines a distance distribution around an entire concept, and positions it cleanly within the existing probabilistic attack framework of Zhang et al. [49] as a strict generalization (|C_ori| = 1 recovers ProbAttack).

The empirical protocol is relatively thorough for an attack paper: targeted attack success on multiple surrogate models (ResNet50, MobileNetV2, ViT-Base), transferability to eight black-box classifiers including adversarially trained ones, a user study for concept preservation, six no-reference image quality metrics, and sensitivity studies over M and |C_ori|.

The proposed data augmentation pipeline (DreamBooth + GPT-4o prompt generation + SDXL LoRA) is a practical contribution for building concept datasets, and the paper is transparent about compute costs, limitations, and broader impacts.
The ablations (Tables 4-5) are informative, e.g., revealing the trade-off between conservative sample selection (higher quality/similarity) and transferability.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is very thin. Theorem 1 is a one-line derivative computation of KL to a Gaussian, and Theorem 2 merely unfolds the definition of KL divergence (the partition function cancels trivially). Neither result requires any genuine mathematical depth, yet they are presented as a central contribution ('theoretical validation').

The empirical support for the core hypothesis (Delta < 0) is statistically weak. In Table 3, many estimated Delta values have standard deviations larger than their magnitude (e.g., bear_plushie: -466.69 +/- 1413.40; wolf_plushie: -325.80 +/- 2811.99; shiny_sneaker: -3203.81 +/- 4447.21; poop_emoji: -219.27 +/- 929.88). The claim that 'Delta < 0 for every concept strongly suggests' the hypothesis is not supported by the reported uncertainties.

The threat model raises fairness concerns. The proposed method requires access to a multi-image dataset of the specific concept plus hours of per-concept diffusion fine-tuning (8 hours/concept on an H100), while baselines operate on a single image. The evaluation therefore compares methods under substantially different assumptions and resource budgets, and the practical attack scenario (attacker possessing a curated concept set) is narrow and not clearly justified.

The evaluation scale is small and the success criteria are lenient: only 26 concepts x 30 target classes (780 examples) on a single dataset, and transferability is measured with a top-100 criterion because top-1 transfer is uniformly low. Top-100/1000 success is a weak notion of a successful targeted attack.

The CLIP similarity results partially contradict the paper's central claim of concept preservation: OURS (CONS) 0.8283 and OURS (AGGR) 0.8043 are worse than ProbAttack (0.8581), and the bolding in Table 2 highlights NCF (0.8728) rather than the proposed method. The paper leans instead on the user study, which involves only five annotators.

The intuition that a broader distance distribution increases overlap with the victim distribution (and thus improves attack success) is largely expected a priori; the empirical gains over a stronger baseline like DiffAttack are mixed (DiffAttack remains better on several black-box models in the ViT-Base setting), weakening the significance of the contribution.

Practicality and reproducibility concerns: the method requires per-concept LoRA training, GPT-4o prompting, and per-image diffusion fine-tuning, with key results (KL estimates, full example sets) deferred to a code repository rather than fully reported; this limits both verifiability and ease of adoption.

strengths: The paper proposes a coherent extension of the probabilistic adversarial attack framework [49] from single images to concepts, and this generalization is formally consistent with prior work (traditional attacks and ProbAttack are special cases), which is a clean conceptual contribution.

The empirical evaluation is broad: multiple victim/surrogate classifiers (ResNet-50, MN-V2, ViT-Base), transferability to defended models (Inception V3 Adv, EfficientNet B7 Adv, ensemble IncRes V2), extensive image-quality metrics, a user study with published annotator instructions, sensitivity studies over M and |Cori|, and qualitative comparisons with a stated policy against cherry-picking.

The empirical KL-divergence study (Table 3) supports the central hypothesis that concept-level distance distributions reduce KL(pdis || pvic), and the theoretical results (Theorems 1–2) give some formal backing to the intuition.
The paper is clearly written and well organized; limitations, compute costs, licenses, and broader impacts are discussed, and code/augmentation details are promised for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is thin. Theorem 1 is elementary calculus (monotonicity of KL against a Gaussian in sigma^2), and Theorem 2 follows directly from the definition of KL divergence. Both rely on idealized assumptions (Gaussian distance distributions with identical means) that do not reflect actual diffusion-model distance distributions, so the theory provides limited insight beyond the intuitive claim that wider distributions overlap more with pvic.

The empirical KL analysis rests on questionable assumptions: likelihood estimation via ELBO is inexact, and the 'likelihood correction' assumes E[log pshare(X)] is equal across the two distributions — an assumption the authors themselves admit may not hold. Several estimated deltas have error bars that include or nearly include zero (e.g., poop_emoji −219 ± 930, wolf_plushie −326 ± 2812), weakening the claimed confirmation.

Fairness of the baseline comparison is a concern. The proposed method draws M=10 samples and selects the best (rejection/sorting), which effectively grants multiple classifier queries; Table 4 shows white-box success for the pure |Cori|=1, M=1 setting is only 26.03%, versus 59.23% for ProbAttack (M=10) and 97.82% for the proposed method — suggesting a substantial part of the gain comes from sample selection and concept-set size rather than the concept-level idea itself. The extra per-concept fine-tuning (~8 hours per concept on an H100) and requirement of a multi-image concept dataset also constitute a much stronger attacker assumption than baselines face, which is not normalized or discussed in the comparison.

The conservative strategy, which is the variant that best preserves the concept, is only 'roughly comparable' to baselines in transferability (e.g., 17.44% vs 20.00% for DiffAttack on Ensemble IncRes V2); the aggressive strategy wins on transferability but degrades concept similarity (CLIP 0.8043 vs ProbAttack 0.8581), creating a trade-off that blunts the headline claim of 'higher success while preserving the concept.'

Evaluation scale is modest: 26 concepts × 30 target classes = 780 adversarial examples, one main white-box victim (appendix results cover others), and the user study uses only five annotators, which limits statistical strength of the concept-preservation claim.

Novelty is incremental relative to ProbAttack [49]: the core sampler is unchanged, and the main additions are (i) replacing the single-image distribution with a concept distribution and (ii) an engineering pipeline (LoRA + GPT-4o prompts + SDXL augmentation) that is competent but not a methodological contribution.

strengths: The concept-level (identity-level) attack framing is a genuinely underexplored setting in unrestricted adversarial attacks, and the paper positions itself well against prior work (Table 3) with a clear probabilistic unification under which ProbAttack is the |C_ori|=1 special case.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: multiple victim architectures (ResNet50, MobileNetV2, ViT-B, ConvNeXt, ResNet50-Adv), transferability to clean and adversarially trained classifiers at Top-1/5/10/100, image-quality metrics, a user study, and full results in the appendix.
Useful ablations: sensitivity to number of samples M and concept-set size |C_ori| (Tables 5-6), estimated KL divergence differences per concept (Table 4), and compute/cost accounting (Table 8).

Good qualitative analysis (Appendix G) with a stated commitment to releasing the complete set of adversarial examples, and a responsible ethics/broader-impact treatment including misuse scenarios and mitigations.
weaknesses: The methodological contribution is thin: the core change is replacing x_ori with C_ori in Eq. (2), which the authors themselves acknowledge. The 'theoretical validation' is oversold — Theorem 1 is a one-line derivative computation of KL for a Gibbs distribution, and Theorem 2 is just the definition of KL; neither provides a meaningful result beyond what is stated.

Fundamental framing concern: the method does not really attack a given input image — it fine-tunes a diffusion model on a curated set of concept images (further augmented by SDXL/GPT-4o) and samples. By construction the samples resemble the concept, so 'concept preservation' is close to circular. It is debatable whether this constitutes an adversarial example of the original image rather than an identity-conditioned generative attack, which changes the problem definition relative to all baselines.

Comparison fairness: the method requires ~8h fine-tuning per concept plus LLM-guided dataset augmentation, while baselines (DiffAttack, ACA, NCF) receive no comparable data/compute budget. White-box success is additionally inflated by best-of-M selection with rejection (M=10), which baselines do not exploit symmetrically.

Unfavorable evidence is downplayed: absolute transferability gains are small (Top-1 transfer ~1-3%); the conservative strategy actually reduces transferability below DiffAttack in several settings; and CLIP similarity of the proposed method (0.8283/0.8043) is lower than ProbAttack and NCF, which sits awkwardly against the concept-preservation narrative.

Theorem 1's applicability condition (E_p[D] > E_q[D]) is asserted to be 'always satisfied' with hand-waving; the KL estimation in Appendix B rests on an unverified equal-expectation assumption for p_share, and the very large variance of the Delta estimates (e.g., ±4447 for shiny_sneaker, ±2334 for duck_toy) makes the 'Delta<0 for every concept' claim statistically fragile.

Scalability and scope: 8h/concept fine-tuning, only 26 concepts and 30 target classes, and a single-dataset (DreamBooth) evaluation limit generality; the requirement of a concept image dataset is a significant practical barrier the limitations section only briefly acknowledges.

Presentation issues: missing repository URL in abstract and reproducibility statement, minor grammatical errors, and some claims (e.g., 'heralds the future of adversarial attacks') exceed what the evidence supports.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and well organized, with the probabilistic framing of replacing a single-image distance distribution with a concept-level distribution being easy to follow.

The empirical evaluation is fairly comprehensive: multiple baselines (NCF, ACA, DiffAttack, ProbAttack), multiple victim classifiers including adversarially trained ones, image quality metrics, and a user study with released instructions.

The ablation on |C_ori| and M (Tables 5-6) and the reported compute costs (Table 8) provide useful transparency, and the appendix materials (hyperparameters, target classes, full result tables) support reproducibility.
The qualitative analysis in Appendix G attempts to substantiate claims about concept preservation rather than relying solely on automated metrics.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is thin. The method is essentially the ProbAttack framework of Zhang et al. (2024b) with the single-image distance distribution replaced by a diffusion model fine-tuned on a set of images of the same object (via DreamBooth-style LoRA + SDXL augmentation). The authors themselves acknowledge the operational change is a one-line substitution (replacing x_ori with C_ori in Eq. 3). This is an incremental extension rather than a substantial methodological advance.

The theoretical results are trivial. Theorem 1 is a one-line derivative of KL divergence with respect to the inverse temperature of a Gibbs distribution, and the required condition E_p[D(X,mu)] > E_q[D(X,mu)] is essentially assumed rather than established for the actual models used. Theorem 2 is a direct algebraic expansion of the KL definition with no content beyond plugging in the victim distribution. Neither theorem analyzes the actual setting (fine-tuned diffusion models, which are not Gibbs distributions of the assumed form), so the 'theoretical validation' claim is overstated.

The empirical KL analysis is unreliable. Estimating KL divergences between image distributions via diffusion model likelihoods in high-dimensional pixel space is known to be problematic (the paper even cites Nalisnick et al. 2019 on likelihood pathologies). Table 4 shows Delta estimates of magnitude ~10^3-10^4 with standard deviations of the same order (e.g., poop emoji: -219 +/- 930; wolf plushie: -326 +/- 2812), so for several concepts the claim that Delta < 0 is not statistically supported. The 'likelihood correction' in Appendix B.2 introduces an unsubstantiated assumption (equal expected p_share likelihoods) that undermines the rigor of the empirical study.

The threat model is questionable and under-justified. The attacker is assumed to possess a curated set of images of the exact target concept, plus ~8 hours of fine-tuning per concept on an H100 to fit the distance distribution. This is a much stronger and more unusual attacker capability than standard adversarial settings, and the paper does not adequately discuss when this capability is realistic or compare against baselines granted comparable resources (e.g., ProbAttack gets only 20 minutes of fine-tuning).

The headline white-box success (97.82%) benefits from a best-of-M selection procedure (M=10 samples with access to the victim classifier for ranking/rejection), which is an extra oracle not granted to the baselines in the same way; this inflates the comparison with DiffAttack (84.23%).

Transferability gains are weak and partially contradictory to the narrative. Absolute top-1 transfer rates are ~1-3% across all methods, and the improvement of OURS (AGGR) over DiffAttack is marginal (e.g., 4.36 vs 4.36 on VGG19, 8.72 vs 8.33 on ResNet152). Moreover, Table 5 shows that increasing M under |C_ori|=30 *decreases* transferability, and Appendix H concedes the method's transferability is far below transferability-optimized methods. The main gains are concentrated in the white-box setting, limiting practical significance.

The aggressive strategy essentially selects samples with the highest target-class softmax probability, which, by the paper's own admission in Appendix H, pushes samples toward injecting target-class semantics - in tension with the stated goal of preserving the original concept. The CONS/AGGR duality makes it unclear which method is actually being proposed.

The concept-preservation evaluation is weak: the user study uses only five annotators, and CLIP scores are inconsistent with the narrative (NCF and clean images score higher than the proposed method on CLIP in Table 2). Identity preservation of fine-tuned diffusion models is also not directly verified against the true original object.

Cost-effectiveness is a concern: 8 hours of fine-tuning per concept versus 20 minutes for the special-case baseline (ProbAttack), and the paper's claim of 'higher attack efficiency' is not supported given this overhead.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and well-motivated, positioning unrestricted adversarial attacks within a probabilistic framework (Zhang et al., 2024b) and cleanly generalizing the distance distribution from a single image to a concept distribution.

The empirical evaluation is fairly comprehensive: multiple surrogate classifiers (ResNet50, MobileNetV2, ViT-B, ConvNeXt, ResNet50-Adv), transferability to both standard and adversarially trained models, six no-reference image quality metrics, a user study, and extensive full results in the appendix (Tables 10-19).
Good ablation analysis: sensitivity of results to M (number of samples) and |C_ori| (Table 5, 6), estimated KL differences per concept (Table 4), and compute cost reporting (Table 8).
The paper includes a thoughtful ethics statement, discussion of mitigation strategies, practical usage guidelines, and a reproducibility statement with released code/data.
Honest discussion of limitations, including the low transferability compared to methods explicitly optimizing for it, and why identity preservation trades off against transferability (Appendix H).
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core contribution is replacing a single-image-centered distance distribution with a concept-centered one (Eq. 2 vs. Eq. 3). The authors themselves acknowledge it is a 'seemingly simple generalization.' The theoretical results do not compensate: Theorem 1 is a one-line derivative computation for Gibbs distributions, and Theorem 2 is essentially the definition of KL divergence; the assumption connecting fine-tuned diffusion models to Gibbs distributions around a concept center is asserted rather than established.

Narrow empirical scope: all experiments are on the DreamBooth dataset (26 object concepts, 780 adversarial examples). Despite the central claim of 'identity-level' attacks, no experiments on human identities or face recognition are presented; all concepts are inanimate objects or animals, leaving the most practically sensitive claim unvalidated.

Fairness of comparison is questionable: the proposed method relies on an expensive pipeline (SDXL+GPT-4o augmentation, ~8h per-concept diffusion fine-tuning, and best-of-M=10 selection with rejection). Baselines like DiffAttack/ACA do not receive an equivalent selection or generation budget, so some of the white-box gains (97.82% vs. 84.23%) may stem from extra compute rather than the conceptual framework.

Absolute transferability numbers are very low (top-1 transfer mostly below 2%, top-5 in the 4-12% range under AGGR). The conservative strategy often performs worse than DiffAttack, so the headline improvement rests on the aggressive strategy, which weakens the concept-preservation guarantee that motivates the paper.

The empirical KL study (Section 5.3) validates only that the per-concept diffusion model has smaller KL to the victim distribution than a single-image model, using variance-reduction assumptions (Appendix B.2) whose reasonableness is argued but not verified; some confidence intervals in Table 4 overlap zero (e.g., wolf plushie, poop emoji).
High practical cost and sensitivity: 8 hours of fine-tuning per concept, careful epoch control to avoid collapse, and dependence on closed models (GPT-4o) complicate reproduction and deployment.

The user study is small (five annotators, only one surrogate setting), and CLIP similarity results are mixed (NCF scores higher CLIP similarity than the proposed method in Table 2), somewhat undercutting the semantic preservation claims.
